name: Tara Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I pick at a car parts distribution centre that supplies garages across the county: brake pads, oil filters, wiper blades, the odd exhaust. Most orders are urgent, because a car's sitting on a ramp waiting, so we have cut-off times every two hours. I pick into blue tubs, check the part number twice, and send it to the van bay. I've been there ten months and I still mix up filters that look the same.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most, and what do you actually like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The cut-offs wear me out, everyone's shouting at once. I like that it's fast and you see the vans go. My boyfriend Josh is a self-employed roofer, so he's out in all weathers, and I do his invoices at night with an AI app. I use AI for pretty much everything, from meal plans to figuring out which filter fits which car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, hype is hype. People should just get on with their work. I'd probably still post that I use AI for Josh's invoices, because it saves me an hour a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job's fine, really. Parts still need picking. The money's what bothers me, I'm on the bottom rate and we've less than a month in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep picking and try to get on the van-bay checks, which pay a bit more. I'd keep using AI for Josh's paperwork, and I'd start pricing up a cheap second-hand van, because I've wanted to run urgent parts to garages myself for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit impatient. I want to be doing my own thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Josh's invoices. How steady is his work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Up and down. Summer's great, winter's slow because nobody wants a roof done in the rain. Last January we lived on my wage alone and it was grim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you see yourself staying in the warehouse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not forever. I'd like my own little courier business, running parts to garages. I know the parts and I know the garages.

Price up a **cheap second-hand van** for a parts courier business.
feel: **Fine but impatient**, wanting to do my own thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to get ahead, not complain. Companies will do what's best for them, and so should we. I'd post about how I'm using AI to run Josh's paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My picking job's safe for a while, robots are slow to spread to small fiddly parts. But the ordering and routing side would change fast. If the company starts routing its own vans with software, there might be room for freelance drivers on the overflow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep picking and buy a second-hand van in the first year if I could get a small loan. I'd start doing weekend parts runs for two local garages. I'd use AI to plan routes and keep the books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but excited. It feels like a door opening a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start the courier business now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once I had the van. Weekends first, then see. I wouldn't quit the warehouse until the weekend parts runs paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary in goods-in. He's fifty-something and hates the scanners. But he's also stubborn, he'd learn if he had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, but people who move fast will be fine. I wouldn't be asking for handouts. I'd be telling friends to start something now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, picking goes around 2031, and maybe driving too, if robots and self-driving vans come in. That's scary. I'd have three years to build something, with no money behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the van straight away and start the parts runs, even with the risk. I'd use AI for everything, to run the business lean. And I'd look at what robots will need, like repairs or installs, in case driving goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited too, but mostly anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work arrive around 2031. Does that hit the courier idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If vans drive themselves, I'm stuffed. So I'd keep an eye on other things, like fitting the robots or servicing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Josh say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Josh would say go for it, but he'd worry about his roofing too. Robots on roofs by 2031? Maybe not, but who knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so use it, and stop waiting for someone to fix it for you. People should start something, even small. I'd say that to the girls at work and at Josh's family dinners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Picking goes around 2034, so the van business would get a few good years before robots and self-driving catch up. That's enough to pay off the van and put something by. I'd watch the self-driving news like a hawk, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the van in year one with a small loan and build up runs for four or five garages. I'd save a slice of every run, maybe 50 a month at first. By year three I'd look at a course in installing or servicing warehouse robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in control. Like a busy cut-off where you know where every part is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. Does the van still make sense if driving might go too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, for a few years. When the self-driving vans are proper, I'd sell mine while it's still worth something and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your backup if it doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robot servicing is my backup. Somebody will need to fix them. I'd rather be on that side of the shelf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say great, plenty of time to build a proper business. People who whinge about robots for ten years and do nothing only have themselves to blame. I'd say that more politely online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fine, I think. Picking would go around 2039, and by then I'd have run the van for years and moved on to something bigger. The thinking AI would only make the paperwork side easier for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year, price the van and get the van-bay checks for the extra money. Next year, buy the van and start the garage runs. After that, grow slowly and add a second van when the first is paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Even excited, though money's still tight now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Is there a risk you'd get comfortable and wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not me. I get bored if I'm not building something. Josh says I'm planning the next thing before the last one's finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you want to be in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2036 I want to be running two vans, maybe three. Josh doing roofs or moved into something less hard on his knees. Kids maybe, once there's money in the bank.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no money to start the van business before everything changes. What would help is a small loan for people starting a business, not a handout, and someone to tell me straight how long vans will still need drivers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about people who want to start something. Everyone treats warehouse workers like we can only be victims of this. Some of us want to build something out of it.
